title: Introductory Microeconomics

pattern.summary: Section A: answer 2 of 4 (20 marks each). Section B: answer 4 of 6 (12 marks each). Section C: answer both (6 marks each). The same paper is set for BA Economics Honours. Diagrams are expected in most answers.

choosing: Section A: a demand–supply equation question (find equilibrium P* and Q*) and a production question (three stages, isoquants) appear almost every time — both are safe.
Section B: price, income and substitution effects (Hicks/Slutsky, Giffen goods) and the labour-market minimum-wage numerical keep returning.
Section C is compulsory: it usually asks market failure/externalities, oligopoly (kinked demand, Stackelberg) or rent — prepare these three.
numerical: Draw a labelled diagram for every answer that has a curve in it — axes, curves, equilibrium point. Diagrams carry a large share of the marks.
For equilibrium questions: set Qd = Qs, solve for P*, then substitute to get Q*. Sketch both lines.
For elasticity: write the formula, substitute, and state whether demand is elastic (> 1), unitary (= 1) or inelastic (< 1).

blocks.title: Welfare, Market Failure and the Role of Government

topics.name: Production: Stages, Isoquants & Returns to Scale
topics.summary: Law of variable proportions (three stages), isoquants and ridge lines, least-cost combination, expansion path, returns to scale, economies of scale.
points: Law of variable proportions (short run, one input variable): Stage I — AP rises (increasing returns); Stage II — AP and MP fall, MP > 0 (rational stage); Stage III — MP negative. A rational producer operates in Stage II.
TP rises at an increasing rate while MP rises, at a decreasing rate when MP falls, and is maximum when MP = 0; MP cuts AP at AP's maximum.
Isoquant: combinations of two inputs giving the same output; slopes down, convex to origin; slope = MRTS.
Ridge lines join points where isoquants turn upward; the area between them is the economic region of production.
Least-cost combination: tangency of isoquant and isocost line — MPL/MPK = w/r (MPL/w = MPK/r).
Expansion path: line joining tangency points as outlay rises; a straight line from the origin for a homogeneous production function.
Returns to scale (long run, all inputs change): increasing, constant, decreasing — seen from isoquant spacing. For Q = AL^a K^b: a + b > 1 IRS, = 1 CRS, < 1 DRS.
Economies of scale: internal (technical, managerial, marketing, financial) and external (industry growth); diseconomies raise LAC.
A production function shows the maximum output from given inputs with given technology; the short run has at least one fixed input, the long run none.
topics.frame: Statement → labelled diagram → explanation of each stage or case → conclusion.
mistakes: Confusing returns to a factor (short run) with returns to scale (long run).

units.title: Production with Two and More Variable Inputs

examples:
Example: the three stages from a table
Workers (L) 1 to 7 on a fixed plot give total product 10, 24, 36, 44, 48, 48, 45.
MP: 10, 14, 12, 8, 4, 0, −3. AP: 10, 12, 12, 11, 9.6, 8, 6.4.
Stage I (AP rising) runs up to 3 workers, where AP peaks at 12. Stage II (AP and MP falling, MP positive) runs from 3 to 6 workers; TP is maximum (48) where MP = 0. Stage III (MP negative) starts after 6 workers. A rational farmer employs between 3 and 6 workers.

Example: returns to scale and least-cost choice
Q = 10L^0.5 K^0.5: exponents add to 1 → constant returns — doubling L and K doubles output. Q = L^0.6 K^0.6: they add to 1.2 → increasing returns.
Least cost: MPL = 20, MPK = 30, wage ₹10, rent ₹20 → MPL/w = 2 but MPK/r = 1.5. The last rupee buys more output through labour, so the firm should use more labour and less capital until the ratios are equal.

topics.name: Income, Substitution & Price Effects
topics.summary: Splitting the price effect (Hicks and Slutsky), inferior and Giffen goods, deriving demand curves.
points: Price effect = substitution effect + income effect.
Substitution effect is always negative (buy more of the cheaper good).
Normal good: income effect reinforces substitution effect. Inferior good: income effect works against it but is weaker. Giffen good: income effect is stronger, so demand rises with price.
Hicks: compensating variation keeps the consumer on the original indifference curve.
Slutsky: cost-difference keeps the original bundle affordable (consumer ends on a higher curve).
Demand curve derived from the price consumption curve (money income constant) or with compensated income (real income constant — Hicksian demand).
topics.frame: Define the three effects → diagram with budget lines and ICs, label points and arrows → explain each move → one-line conclusion for the good type.
mistakes: Drawing the compensated budget line not parallel to the new one.
examples:
Example: splitting a price effect
The price of tea falls from ₹20 to ₹10 a cup and a consumer's purchases rise from 4 to 7 cups a week (price effect +3).
Take away just enough income to put them back on their old indifference curve (Hicks): they would buy 6 cups → substitution effect +2. The remaining +1 is the income effect → tea is a normal good.
If instead the income effect were −1 (total +1), tea would be inferior; if it were −3 (total −1, buying less at a lower price), it would be a Giffen good.

topics.name: Demand, Supply, Equilibrium & Tax Incidence
topics.summary: Equilibrium from equations, shifts, price ceilings and floors, consumer/producer surplus, tax burden and deadweight loss.
points: Demand Q = a − bP slopes down; supply Q = c + dP slopes up.
Equilibrium where Qd = Qs.
Change in price of a substitute moves demand the same way; of a complement, the opposite way.
Price ceiling below equilibrium → shortage; price floor above equilibrium → surplus.
Tax incidence: the more inelastic side bears more of the tax. Perfectly elastic demand → sellers bear it all; perfectly elastic supply → buyers bear it all.
Deadweight loss: the lost surplus from trades that no longer happen after a tax.

Change in quantity demanded (movement along the curve) comes from the good's own price; change in demand (shift of the curve) comes from income, tastes, prices of related goods and expectations. The same applies to supply.
A tax on land (fixed supply) falls wholly on landowners — the rent paid by users does not change.
method: Set Qd = Qs and solve for P*.
Substitute P* into either equation for Q*.
Consumer surplus = ½ × (max price − P*) × Q*; producer surplus = ½ × (P* − min price) × Q* for straight lines.
formula: a − bP = c + dP → P* = (a − c)/(b + d)
mistakes: Forgetting to draw the diagram with the equilibrium marked.
examples:
Example: equilibrium, surplus and a tax
Qd = 100 − 2P and Qs = −20 + 2P. Setting 100 − 2P = −20 + 2P gives P* = ₹30 and Q* = 40.
Consumer surplus = ½ × (50 − 30) × 40 = 400; producer surplus = ½ × (30 − 10) × 40 = 400.
A ₹4 tax per unit on sellers: new supply Qs = −28 + 2P → P = ₹32, Q = 36. Buyers pay ₹2 more and sellers get ₹2 less (₹28) — shared equally because the two curves are equally steep. Tax revenue = 4 × 36 = 144; deadweight loss = ½ × 4 × 4 = 8.

Example: a price ceiling
With the same curves, a ceiling of ₹25 makes Qd = 50 but Qs = 30 → a shortage of 20 units, leading to queues, rationing or black markets.

topics.name: Monopolistic Competition & Oligopoly
topics.summary: Excess capacity, kinked demand curve, Cournot and Stackelberg models, prisoner's dilemma.
points: Monopolistic competition: many firms, differentiated products, free entry; long-run tangency of AR with LAC on its falling part → excess capacity.
Kinked demand curve (Sweezy): rivals match price cuts but not rises → kink at current price, gap in MR → price rigidity. Limitation: does not explain how the price was set.
Cournot: each firm chooses quantity taking rival's output as given; equilibrium where reaction curves cross.
Stackelberg: leader moves first knowing the follower's reaction — first-mover advantage.
Prisoner's dilemma: each player's dominant strategy leads to a worse joint outcome (e.g. cartel cheating).
Oligopoly: a few interdependent firms. Firms may behave non-cooperatively (Cournot, Stackelberg) or cooperate.
Cartel: firms agree jointly on output and price to act like a monopolist (e.g. OPEC); each member is tempted to cheat by producing more, which makes cartels unstable.
method: Cournot (linear demand P = a − bQ, equal cost c): each firm q = (a − c)/(3b).
Stackelberg: leader q₁ = (a − c)/(2b); follower q₂ = (a − c)/(4b).
mistakes: Drawing the kinked MR without the vertical gap.

units.title: Monopolistic Competition: Price and Output Decisions

examples:
Example: Cournot vs Stackelberg vs monopoly
Market demand P = 100 − Q; each firm's marginal cost ₹10.
Cournot: each firm makes (100 − 10)/3 = 30; total 60; price ₹40.
Stackelberg: the leader makes 90/2 = 45, the follower 90/4 = 22.5; total 67.5; price ₹32.50 — the leader gains by moving first.
If the two formed a cartel and acted as one monopolist: total 45, price ₹55. Under perfect competition: price ₹10, output 90.

Example: prisoner's dilemma in a cartel
Two cement firms agree to restrict output and each earn ₹10 crore. If one secretly produces more while the other keeps to the deal, the cheat earns ₹14 crore and the other ₹4 crore. Whatever the other does, cheating pays more, so both cheat and each earns ₹6 crore — worse for both than sticking to the deal. This is why cartels tend to break down.

topics.name: Perfect Competition
topics.summary: Short- and long-run equilibrium, shutdown point, supply curve, efficiency and the role of marginal cost.
points: Features: many buyers and sellers, homogeneous product, free entry and exit, perfect knowledge; firm is a price-taker (P = AR = MR).
Equilibrium: MC = MR and MC rising.
Short run: firm may earn profit or loss; it continues if P ≥ AVC. Shutdown point: P = minimum AVC.
Supply curve of the firm = rising part of MC above minimum AVC.
Long run: P = MR = MC = minimum LAC — normal profit, optimal capacity, productive and allocative efficiency (P = MC).
A firm operating at a loss may stay open in the short run if it covers variable costs and part of fixed costs.
Break-even point: P = minimum ATC (normal profit only). Market supply is the horizontal sum of the firms' supply curves.
method: Profit maximisation: set P = MC, solve for q, check MC is rising; profit = TR − TC.

units.title: Perfect Competition: Firm and Industry Equilibrium

examples:
Example: a price-taking firm
TC = 100 + 10q + q², so MC = 10 + 2q. The market price is ₹50.
Set P = MC: 50 = 10 + 2q → q = 20. TR = 1,000; TC = 100 + 200 + 400 = 700 → profit ₹300.
ATC = 100/q + 10 + q is lowest at q = 10, where it is ₹30. At P = ₹30 the firm earns only normal profit (break-even). AVC = 10 + q is at least ₹10, so the firm shuts down if the price falls below ₹10.

topics.name: Labour Market & Rent
topics.summary: Labour demand/supply numericals with minimum wage, backward-bending supply, wage differences, and theories of rent.
points: Labour supply from labour–leisure choice; backward-bending at high wages when the income effect outweighs the substitution effect.
A minimum wage above equilibrium reduces employment to labour demanded at that wage (unemployment = Ls − Ld).
Wage differences: skill and training, risk, non-monetary benefits, trade unions, discrimination, immobility.
Ricardian rent: payment for the original, indestructible powers of the soil; arises from differences in fertility and scarcity.
Modern theory: economic rent = earnings above transfer earnings, for any factor.
Quasi-rent (Marshall): short-run surplus earned by machines and other factors fixed in the short run.

Marginal productivity theory: a factor's reward is set by its marginal product; firms hire a factor until its marginal revenue product (MRP) equals its price. Under perfect competition MRP = VMP = MP × price of output.
Demand for a factor is derived demand — it comes from the demand for the goods it helps to make.
Labour unions bargain for higher wages; a union wage above equilibrium works like a minimum wage — higher pay for those employed but fewer jobs.
method: Equilibrium wage: set Ld = Ls. With a minimum wage W̄: employment = Ld(W̄).
formula: Economic rent = actual earnings − transfer earnings
examples:
Example: wage and a minimum wage
Ld = 100 − 2W and Ls = 20 + 2W → equilibrium wage ₹20, employment 60.
A minimum wage of ₹25: firms hire only 50 (Ld), while 70 want work (Ls) → 20 unemployed.
Marginal productivity: if the 5th worker adds 4 units, each sold at ₹50, their MRP is ₹200; at a wage of ₹200 the firm hires up to the 5th worker.

Example: economic rent
A popular singer earns ₹10 lakh a year; their best alternative, teaching music, pays ₹3 lakh (transfer earnings). Economic rent = 10 − 3 = ₹7 lakh — the surplus above what keeps them in this job.

topics.name: Welfare, Market Failure & Externalities
topics.summary: Pareto efficiency and welfare theorems, sources of market failure, externalities, public goods, asymmetric information.
points: Pareto efficiency: no one can be made better off without making someone worse off; needs efficiency in exchange, production and product mix.
First fundamental theorem: a competitive equilibrium is Pareto efficient.
Sources of market failure: market power, externalities, public goods, incomplete/asymmetric information.
Externality: a cost or benefit to third parties. Remedies: Pigouvian tax (negative) or subsidy (positive), regulation, tradable permits, Coase bargaining.
Public goods: non-rival and non-excludable (e.g. street lights) → free-rider problem. Merit goods: under-consumed if left to the market (e.g. education).
Asymmetric information: adverse selection (before the deal — Akerlof's 'lemons') and moral hazard (after the deal — insured drivers taking more risk).
With an externality, marginal social cost = marginal private cost + marginal external cost (MSC = MPC + MEC); the market over-produces goods with external costs.

Government remedies in the book: Pigouvian taxes and subsidies, direct regulation (price ceilings on stents and essential medicines, safety standards, pollution permits, advertising bans) and private bargaining.
topics.frame: Definition → causes or types as headed points → diagram (MSC vs MPC for externality) → remedy → example.

units.title: Welfare: Allocative Efficiency under Perfect Competition
Efficiency of the Market Mechanism: Market Failure and the Role of the State

examples:
Example: pollution and a Pigouvian tax
Demand for a chemical: P = 100 − Q. A factory's private marginal cost is ₹40 a unit, but each unit causes ₹10 of pollution damage, so MSC = ₹50.
The market produces where P = MPC: Q = 60. The social optimum is where P = MSC: Q = 50. The extra 10 units create a deadweight loss of ½ × 10 × 10 = ₹50.
A tax of ₹10 a unit (equal to the external cost) makes the factory produce 50.

Example: asymmetric information
Adverse selection: in a used-car market, sellers know which cars are 'lemons' but buyers do not, so buyers offer an average price; owners of good cars withdraw, and mostly lemons are left.
Moral hazard: after buying full theft insurance, a person stops locking their bike carefully.

topics.name: Cost Curves (Short & Long Run)
topics.summary: LAC as the envelope of SAC curves, LMC vs SMC, economies of scale and the shape of LAC, economic vs accounting profit.
points: Short run: fixed and variable costs; AFC falls continuously; AVC, ATC and MC are U-shaped; MC cuts AVC and ATC at their minima.
LAC is the envelope of SAC curves — tangent to each, U-shaped due to economies then diseconomies of scale.
LMC cuts LAC at its minimum; at each output, LMC equals the SMC of the plant tangent there.
Fixed costs do not affect the profit-maximising output (MC = MR) but do affect total profit.
Accounting profit = revenue − explicit costs; economic profit = revenue − explicit − implicit (opportunity) costs.
Costs can be explicit (paid out) or implicit (opportunity cost of own resources); private cost vs social cost matters when there are externalities.
topics.frame: Statement → diagram with SAC curves and LAC envelope (or LMC/SMC) → explanation → conclusion.
mistakes: Drawing LAC through the minimum of every SAC (it touches only the minimum of the optimal plant).
examples:
Example: short-run cost table
Fixed cost ₹100; variable cost for output 1 to 5: 40, 70, 90, 120, 170.
TC: 140, 170, 190, 220, 270. MC: 40, 30, 20, 30, 50.
AVC: 40, 35, 30, 30, 34 — lowest (30) at 3–4 units, where MC also equals 30.
ATC: 140, 85, 63.3, 55, 54 — still falling because MC (50) is below ATC.
AFC: 100, 50, 33.3, 25, 20 — falls continuously.

Example: accounting vs economic profit
A shop's revenue is ₹10 lakh and its explicit costs are ₹6 lakh → accounting profit ₹4 lakh. The owner could earn ₹3 lakh in a job and ₹50,000 interest on the capital invested (implicit costs) → economic profit only ₹50,000.

topics.name: Elasticity of Demand & Supply
topics.summary: Price, income and cross elasticity; point and midpoint methods; determinants; elasticity and marginal revenue.
points: Price elasticity of demand: % change in quantity ÷ % change in price.
Determinants: availability of substitutes, necessity vs luxury, share of income, time period, number of uses.
Income elasticity: > 1 luxury, 0–1 necessity, < 0 inferior; 0 means demand does not respond to income.
Cross elasticity: positive for substitutes, negative for complements.
Point elasticity on a straight-line demand curve = lower segment ÷ upper segment.
Elasticity of supply depends on time, spare capacity, ease of storing, and factor mobility.

The book measures price elasticity by the point (percentage) method, the total expenditure (outlay) method and the geometric method. Total expenditure method: if spending rises when price falls, e > 1; unchanged, e = 1; falls, e < 1.
method: Midpoint (arc): e = [(Q₂ − Q₁)/((Q₂ + Q₁)/2)] ÷ [(P₂ − P₁)/((P₂ + P₁)/2)].
From total revenue R(Q): MR = dR/dQ, then use MR = P(1 − 1/e).
mistakes: Dropping the minus sign without saying you use absolute values.
examples:
Example: point and arc elasticity
Q = 100 − 2P at P = ₹20: Q = 60, so e = 2 × 20/60 = 0.67 (inelastic).
Arc: price rises from ₹10 to ₹12 and quantity falls from 100 to 80. e = (20/90) ÷ (2/11) = 1.22 (elastic). Check with total spending: 10 × 100 = ₹1,000 falls to 12 × 80 = ₹960 when the price rises — spending falls, so demand is elastic.
At P = ₹20 with e = 2, MR = 20 × (1 − 1/2) = ₹10.

Example: income and cross elasticity
Income rises 10%: restaurant meals rise 20% (income elasticity 2 → luxury); rice rises 3% (0.3 → necessity); coarse grain falls 5% (−0.5 → inferior).
Tea's price rises 10% and coffee demand rises 5% → cross elasticity +0.5 (substitutes). Petrol's price rises and demand for cars falls → negative (complements).

topics.name: Cardinal Utility & Consumer Surplus
topics.summary: Law of diminishing marginal utility, equi-marginal utility, consumer equilibrium, deriving demand, consumer surplus.
points: Cardinal approach: utility measurable in units (utils); assumptions include constant marginal utility of money and independent utilities.
Law of diminishing marginal utility: each extra unit gives less satisfaction; exceptions include money, hobbies, addictive goods.
One-good equilibrium: MUx = Px (in money terms). Two goods: MUx/Px = MUy/Py (equi-marginal utility).
Demand curve from DMU: as price falls, more units satisfy MU = P.
Consumer surplus (Marshall): what the consumer is willing to pay minus what they actually pay — area under demand above price.
Criticism: utility is not measurable; MU of money is not constant; ignores income effect; cannot explain Giffen goods.
method: From total utility, find MU for each unit; buy up to the unit where MU ≥ price.
examples:
Example: how many mangoes, and the consumer surplus
MU of successive mangoes (in ₹): 20, 16, 12, 8, 4. Price ₹10 each.
Buy while MU ≥ price → 3 mangoes (the 4th is worth only ₹8).
Consumer surplus = what they would pay (20 + 16 + 12 = 48) − what they pay (3 × 10 = 30) = ₹18.
If the price falls to ₹8, they buy 4 — this is how the downward-sloping demand curve follows from diminishing marginal utility.

topics.name: Monopoly & Price Discrimination
topics.summary: Monopoly equilibrium, no supply curve, deadweight loss, price discrimination, public monopoly pricing, mark-up pricing.
points: Monopoly: single seller, no close substitutes, barriers to entry; downward-sloping AR with MR below it.
Equilibrium MR = MC; a monopolist never produces on the inelastic part of demand (MR would be negative).
No supply curve: the same price can go with different quantities depending on demand.
Deadweight loss: output lower and price higher than under perfect competition.
Price discrimination: 1st degree (each unit at maximum price), 2nd degree (by quantity blocks), 3rd degree (different markets; higher price where demand is less elastic).
Public monopoly: marginal-cost pricing (efficient but may cause loss) vs average-cost pricing (no loss, less efficient).
Mark-up pricing: price = AVC + percentage mark-up.
Compared with perfect competition, monopoly gives a higher price, lower output and P > MC — hence allocative inefficiency and a deadweight loss.
topics.frame: Definition → diagram (AR, MR, MC, AC with the profit area) → explanation → comparison with perfect competition.
examples:
Example: monopoly vs competition
Demand P = 100 − Q; MC = ₹20 (constant).
Monopoly: MR = 100 − 2Q = 20 → Q = 40, P = ₹60, profit (60 − 20) × 40 = ₹1,600.
Perfect competition would give P = MC = ₹20 and Q = 80.
Deadweight loss of monopoly = ½ × (60 − 20) × (80 − 40) = ₹800.

Example: third-degree price discrimination
MC ₹10. In market A demand elasticity is 2; in market B it is 4. Using MR = P(1 − 1/e) = MC: P_A = 10 ÷ 0.5 = ₹20; P_B = 10 ÷ 0.75 = ₹13.33. The higher price is charged where demand is less elastic — like higher fares for business travellers.

topics.name: Indifference Curve Analysis
topics.summary: Indifference curves and budget line, consumer equilibrium, PCC/ICC/Engel curve, corner solutions.
points: Indifference curve: bundles giving equal satisfaction; slopes down, convex to origin (diminishing MRS), never intersect, higher is better.
Budget line: Px·X + Py·Y = M; slope = −Px/Py.
Equilibrium: tangency, MRSxy = Px/Py, and the IC must be convex — otherwise tangency is not optimal.
Corner solution: only one good bought (e.g. concave ICs or perfect substitutes).
Price consumption curve (PCC) traces equilibria as price changes → demand curve. Income consumption curve (ICC) as income changes → Engel curve.
Perfect substitutes → straight-line ICs; perfect complements → L-shaped ICs.
The ordinal approach only ranks bundles (first, second…) instead of measuring utility; the indifference map shows the consumer's whole scale of preferences.
topics.frame: Assumptions → diagram → conditions for equilibrium → conclusion.
examples:
Example: consumer equilibrium
Income ₹100; Px = ₹10, Py = ₹5. Budget line: 10X + 5Y = 100 (at most 10 X or 20 Y); slope −2.
With U = XY, MRS = Y/X. Equilibrium where MRS = Px/Py → Y/X = 2 → Y = 2X. Then 10X + 10X = 100 → X = 5, Y = 10.
If Px falls to ₹5: Y/X = 1 → X = 10, Y = 10. Joining such points gives the price consumption curve, from which the demand curve for X follows (price 10 → 5 units; price 5 → 10 units).

topics.name: PPC, Scarcity & Basic Concepts
topics.summary: Production possibility curve, central problems, scarcity and choice, micro vs macro, positive vs normative.
points: PPC: combinations of two goods an economy can produce with given resources and technology, fully and efficiently used.
Concave to the origin because opportunity cost increases; a straight line if cost is constant.
Point inside = unemployment or inefficiency; on the curve = efficient; outside = unattainable.
Shifts outward with more resources or better technology; unemployment does not shift it — the economy moves inside.
Central problems: what, how and for whom to produce, plus efficiency and growth.
Micro vs macro: individual units vs the whole economy. Positive (what is) vs normative (what ought to be). Static vs dynamic analysis. Stock (at a point) vs flow (over time).
Scarcity: wants are unlimited but resources are limited and have alternative uses — so every society must choose, and every choice has an opportunity cost.
topics.frame: Definition → PPC diagram with points labelled → explanation → conclusion.
examples:
Example: a PPC schedule and increasing opportunity cost
Butter 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 with guns 15, 14, 12, 9, 5, 0.
Each extra unit of butter costs 1, 2, 3, 4, then 5 guns — rising opportunity cost, so the PPC is concave to the origin.
Producing 2 butter and 8 guns is inside the curve (it could make 12 guns) → unemployment or waste. 4 butter and 9 guns is outside → unattainable with present resources; better technology would shift the curve out.
